lead: This week the first readings come from Paul’s Letter to the Philippians and the Gospels from Luke’s journey to Jerusalem. Today Paul sings of Christ who emptied himself and was exalted, and Jesus tells of a great dinner whose first guests make excuses. The one who humbled himself is the host who fills his house with the humble.

set: Paul writes to the church at Philippi, a Roman colony in Macedonia and the first church he founded in Europe (Acts 16). He writes from prison, either in Rome (about AD 61–62) or, as some think, in Ephesus a few years earlier. The community is generous but troubled by rivalry, so Paul asks them to look to the interests of others (2:3–4) and then gives the supreme example: Christ. Many scholars think verses 6–11 are an early Christian hymn that Paul quotes or composed.
str: v. 5: the call: have the same mind as Christ.
vv. 6–8: the descent: form of God, form of a slave, death on a cross.
vv. 9–11: the ascent: God exalts him and gives him the name above every name.
kw: Not an outward appearance but the reality of being God. He did not stop being God when he took “the form of a slave”.
From this verb comes the word kenosis. The Son did not empty himself of his divinity but of its glory and privileges, by taking our humanity.
Something to be held on to or used for one’s own advantage. Many readers see a contrast with Adam, who grasped at being like God: Christ did not use his equality with God for himself.
vv: but emptied himself, taking the form of a slave, being born in human likeness.
he humbled himself and became obedient to the point of death

Crucifixion was the death reserved for slaves and rebels, a punishment so shameful that Roman citizens, as many of the Philippians were, were normally exempt from it. Paul places it at the lowest point of the hymn.
so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bend, in heaven and on earth and under the earth, and every tongue should confess that Jesus Christ is Lord,
An echo of Isaiah 45:23, where God says, “To me every knee shall bow, every tongue shall swear.” What Isaiah says of the Lord, Paul says of Jesus: “Lord” (kyrios) is the name of God.
ch: The Catechism quotes this hymn when it teaches the Incarnation (CCC 461) and when it explains that the first confessions of faith gave Jesus the divine title “Lord” (CCC 449). The Church has always held that in emptying himself the Son remained fully God while becoming fully man: this is the faith of the Council of Chalcedon (451). The hymn is sung every Saturday evening in Evening Prayer of the Liturgy of the Hours.

r.h: Come, for everything is ready now
set: Jesus is at a Sabbath dinner in the house of a leader of the Pharisees (14:1). He has just told his host to invite “the poor, the crippled, the lame, and the blind” (14:13). A guest responds with a pious remark about the banquet of the kingdom, and Jesus answers with a parable. In that culture an important host sent a first invitation and then, when the meal was ready, a servant to call the guests.
str: v. 15: “Blessed is anyone who will eat bread in the kingdom of God!”
vv. 16–17: the invitation and the call.
vv. 18–20: three excuses: land, oxen, marriage.
vv. 21–23: the poor and the disabled of the town, then those on the roads outside.
v. 24: none of the first guests will taste the dinner.
kw: The banquet is a common biblical image of the kingdom (Isaiah 25:6).
Literally “to ask to be let off”. The excuses are polite, and each concerns a good thing. But each puts something else before the host.
Not force but urgent, insistent hospitality: in the East a humble person would refuse an invitation at first and had to be pressed to come.
vv: The time of the kingdom has come in Jesus. Nothing remains to be prepared except the guests’ answer.
‘Go out at once into the streets and lanes of the town and bring in the poor, the crippled, the blind, and the lame.’
The same four groups as in 14:13. The host does what Jesus has just asked the Pharisee to do.
and compel people to come in, so that my house may be filled.
The host wants a full house. Luke’s readers saw here the mission to the nations beyond Israel.
ch: Before Communion the priest says, “Blessed are those called to the supper of the Lamb” (compare Revelation 19:9). Every Mass is this invitation. St Augustine once used “compel them to come in” to justify pressure on the Donatists; the Church today teaches clearly that no one may be forced to embrace the faith (Dignitatis Humanae 10). The compulsion of the parable is the urgency of love.

qa: Did Christ stop being God when he “emptied himself”?
No. He took on what he was not, our human nature, without losing what he was. He “humbled himself”: the emptying was a choice of love, not a loss of divinity (CCC 464, 469).
study: Philippians 2:5 asks us to have the mind of Christ. In which relationship do I most need his humility?
Which good thing (my “field”, my “oxen”) most often becomes my excuse not to come to the Lord’s table?
